london.population: The study records 216,943 residents across 21.8 km² of the neighbourhood.
london.location: Camden sits within inner London and represents one of the city’s most distinctive neighbourhoods for studying the relationship between historical layers, mixed use streets, and a fine grain urban structure. It is known for its dense but walkable blocks, strong civic presence, and vibrant high streets that act as social and economic anchors. Camden’s combination of industrial heritage, rail infrastructure, and diverse street life makes it a rich reference for neighbourhoods shaped by incremental change rather than large scale masterplanning.
london.history: Originally a semi rural edge settlement, Camden urbanised rapidly in the 19th century with the arrival of the Regent’s Canal and extensive rail infrastructure. The area became a hub for warehouses, workshops, and Victorian housing, later attracting cultural uses and markets through the 20th century. Camden’s development is characterised by layering of industrial foundations overlaid with residential streets, followed by contemporary cultural and commercial uses.
london.green-space: Green space in Camden is structured around small parks, canal edges, and residual landscape pockets embedded within the dense urban fabric. Regent’s Canal functions as a linear green corridor supporting walking and cycling, while spaces like Regent’s Park nearby provide larger recreational landscapes. Within neighbourhood blocks, smaller gardens and tree-lined streets soften the density and contribute to Camden’s distinctive urban greenery character.
london.transport: Camden is shaped by robust multi-modal transport: underground lines (Northern Line), overground stations, buses, and the canal towpath create layered mobility. The rail viaducts and station clusters generate intensification and distinct grains on either side, with tighter residential plots to the west and more commercial blocks toward transport nodes. The area’s heavy pedestrian flows around the station underpin the intensity of street activity and support a strong high street economy.
london.building-use: Camden’s mixed-use buildings are concentrated around its main streets. Ground floors host shops, cafés, music venues, and workshops, while upper floors shift to offices or residential uses. The area is known for cultural institutions such as markets, studios and galleries that are embedded directly into the everyday street fabric. This blend produces a lively public realm with continuous active edges and many transitions between public, semi-public, and private space.
london.character: Camden’s character is defined by fine grain Victorian terraces, industrial brick warehouses, and narrow commercial frontages that create rich street edges. Regular rhythms of windows and shopfronts maintain walkability and human scale. Warehouse typologies with large openings mark former industrial areas, while residential streets feature consistent brick façades, bay windows, and modest heights. The contrast between these two grains is central to Camden’s identity and urban legibility.
london.room: The typical residential typology consists of narrow terraced houses with stacked rooms and small rear gardens, later adapted into flats. In warehouse conversions, deep floorplates allow for flexible live & work arrangements. The neighbourhood also includes mansion blocks, larger brick buildings with shared stairwells and repeated flat layouts offering higher-density living without high-rise construction. These room structures illustrate Camden’s incremental intensification through subdivision, extension, and adaptive reuse.

berlin.population: The study records 168,947 residents across 10.96 km² of the neighbourhood.
berlin.location: Berlin is a fascinating city to explore and to live in. It has a multicultural character and its own unique lifestyle. A place with a sense of community that creates a feeling of belonging even for those who aren’t officially a part of it. Prenzlauer Berg, with one of the highest density rates of the city, maintains these qualities alive within its vibrant life. This is further supported by social engagement, infrastructural system, and green public spaces.
berlin.history: The foundations of contemporary Berlin started to develop in the 18th century. From a walled city, it expanded rapidly with industrialisation, population growth and the introduction of railways and factories. Prenzlauer Berg was formed as a working-class expansion in the 19th century while the city witnessed a social and cultural boom. While during World War II most of the city was destroyed by bombing, Prenzlauer Berg has seen minor damages. It became a border-neighbourhood on the east side of the Wall with buildings neglected over Soviet occupation. Developing into an artistic enclave with cheap housing and vicinity to the Mitte, from the 90’s it became a symbol for gentrification.
berlin.green-space: The quality of life in Prenzlauer Berg is enhanced by the huge presence of green spaces. Majorly consisting of public greenery with parks, arbored streets, green pockets and squares. Neighbourhood still hosts private courtyards which have plenty of vegetation. The richness of natural environment has a permanent presence of everyday urban life.
berlin.transport: Prenzlauer Berg offers plenty of public transport choices which blend with the urban environment. From underground to railway systems, from buses to trains, it allows one to reach any point in the city and move through it with ease.
berlin.building-use: Along the main streets, most of the buildings are mixed use, while entire blocks have a predominant residential use. Later-developed areas accommodate buildings for leisure and entertainment. Some spots are purely commercial, providing Prenzlauer Berg with a good balance between life, services and work.
berlin.character: Historic Wilhelmine buildings wrap public spaces hosting street art and an abundance of greenery. The place feels alive with a clam street life. The neighbourhood has a unique past to tell - poverty, decay, and resistance now transformed into an optimised and overly priced setting. It’s a place with social and cultural heart which has fostered a community that makes one feel welcomed.
berlin.room: The floor plan shows a classic two-bedroom Altbau (old building) apartment, irregular and generous in some parts, while compressed in others. The generous entrance acts as a spatial buffer between the two bedrooms, the living room, and the kitchen. The latter one grants access to facilities and a studio. Facades and a solid structure add the historical charm, with high ceilings, ornate stucco and large windows. The interiors are adapted into a more minimalist look that reinterprets the space.

zaragoza.population: The study records 50,115 residents across 3.02 km² of the neighbourhood.
zaragoza.location: The Universidad neighbourhood exhibits a highly diverse urban form while remaining coherently structured around a walkable boulevard and a vibrant public square. A key element of its distinctiveness lies in the boulevard’s capacity to draw people into the area. Although it serves as a major transit corridor - particularly through its tram connection to the city centre - it functions predominantly as a pedestrian-oriented avenue. This pedestrian emphasis fosters active commercial uses and supports a lively urban atmosphere throughout the surrounding streets.
zaragoza.history: Zaragoza is a city historically anchored by the Cathedral of El Pilar, whose monumental presence along the river laid the foundation for the dense fabric of the old town. During the 1920s, the city initiated a significant phase of expansion and established a new civic centre intended to guide its future growth. From this centre, five major avenues and boulevards were planned to expand outward, structuring subsequent urban development. It is within this context that the neighbourhood of Universidad emerged, largely shaped by planning schemes formulated in the 1930s, which continue to define its urban form today.
zaragoza.green-space: The neighbourhood contains the largest park in the city, which functions as its principal hub for recreation and physical activity. In addition to extensive green space, the park accommodates a wide range of sport facilities and public swimming pools, supporting diverse forms of exercise. It also serves as a major venue for events and community activities, drawing residents from across Zaragoza and reinforcing the neighbourhood’s role as an important recreational destination.
zaragoza.transport: The neighbourhood’s transportation system is relatively straightforward, structured primarily along the central boulevard where the tram serves as the main mode of transit. This line provides a direct connection between the neighbourhood and the city centre. Complementing the tram corridor, several perpendicular bus routes extend through the area, linking it to additional destinations across the city and enhancing overall network accessibility.
zaragoza.building-use: The neighbourhood is composed predominantly of mixed-use apartment buildings, many of which incorporate commercial spaces at street level. This built form strongly shapes the area’s urban identity. In addition to residential and commercial functions, the neighbourhood accommodates part of the University of Zaragoza campus, the Real Zaragoza football stadium, and one of the city’s principal hospitals. Together, these elements contribute to a highly diverse mix of activities and demographic groups, reinforcing the neighbourhood’s multifunctional character.
zaragoza.character: The character of the neighbourhood is fundamentally shaped by its central boulevard, which concentrates much of the area’s activity and distributes it into the surrounding perpendicular streets. The avenue hosts children’s play areas, temporary or seasonal kiosks and a series of pauses in the urban fabric. Small squares, green spaces, cafés and bars provide opportunities for leisure. These spaces are continuously activated by pedestrian movement along the boulevard, reinforcing its role as the primary social and spatial spine of the neighbourhood.
zaragoza.room: Standard flats are family-oriented with a large number of bedrooms and generous communal spaces. The housing blocks are organized around a main courtyard that splits the block in the middle, allowing both sides of the flats to receive natural sunlight and ventilation. The dining room or larger communal spaces usually face the street. In addition, smaller courtyards are incorporated, typically serving the bedrooms. These spaces allow for ventilation but receive limited direct sunlight in order to reduce excessive heat during the summer months.

tokyo.population: The study records 35,775 residents across 1.27 km² of the neighbourhood.
tokyo.location: Tokyo is a highly dense megacity, an ideal reference for analysing neighbourhood form under extreme population pressure. It consists of small plots with short blocks and layered public spaces underground. Ikebukuro is a transit-oriented district built around one of Tokyo’s busiest stations. Large crowds of roughly 2 million passengers daily move through linked concourses and streets, keeping the area active all day.
tokyo.history: The area began as farmland and grew quickly after the opening of the railway station in 1903. It was heavily damaged during the war. Over the last century, dense rebuilding has been concentrated around major commercial and entertainment facilities. Currently it’s known as one of Tokyo’s main transport hubs and urban centre for cultural attractions and retail.
tokyo.green-space: Most green spaces in the area are in small pockets, school grounds, and rooftop gardens. In 2019 the renewal of Ikebukuro Nishiguchi Park into Global Ring added shade, seating, and a geometric outdoor stage that visually links to Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre and Metropolitan Plaza. Sound and digital art unify the park and encourage visits.
tokyo.transport: Ikebukuro is one of Tokyo’s busiest transport centres, anchored by a large station with 26 platforms. Bus stops cluster around the station, with Sunshine City as the major transfer point. Every day, significant number of passengers use it as their commute network.
tokyo.building-use: Buildings near the station have mostly commercial, cultural and leisure purposes. Mixed-use towers are based on retail units with hotels, cinemas, clinics and department stores. Residential areas become more prominent as one moves outward, with mid-rise blocks on quieter streets.
tokyo.character: Ikebukuro Station’s ground floor doubles as a street of cafés, restaurants, and shops, attracting workers, students, and visitors through all day. Limited parking and green spaces with seating encourage pedestrian circulation. The opposite blocks layer active retail at ground level with offices above.
tokyo.room: Typical apartments are compact, with small bedrooms and short corridors. A multipurpose room combines living, cooking and dining. A genkan entry, typically a sunken area at the entrance, holds storage and services. It leads into a galley kitchen and prefabricated bath, where sliding partitions create privacy.

glasgow.population: The study records 25,371 residents across 0.96 km² of the neighbourhood.
glasgow.location: Neighbourhood of Hillhead is one of the busiest areas of Glasgow, Scotland’s most populated town. It features grandeur of sandstone Victorian and Arts and Crafts houses contrasting with postindustrial redevelopment. Hillhead has stepped aside from modernist infusion and preserved the spirit of old town, which prescribed its popularity and avant-garde kitsch.
glasgow.history: Referring to its name, it started with a prominent Hillhead house with a view over Kelvin in 18th century. Land just started to divide into plots for villas and terraced housing. Major changes happened between 1850 - 1900 with UOG campuses and Kelvingrove museum establishment, when area was connected to town via Great Western Road.
glasgow.green-space: Kelvingrove park is crucial to the character of Hillhead. It became a popular landscape spot and an oasis to take tension away from the busy streets. River Kelvin serpents through the site, with pedestrian paths running along its bank. Many of the old tenements are capturing semi-private green courtyards which highlights Hillhead’s focus on landscaping.
glasgow.transport: Two major car routes corner Hillhead’s periphery - Byres and Great Western Road. The latter connects neighborhood with central town via cars and buses. Hillhead has its own underground station which effortlessly transfers passengers within simple inner and outer Glasgow circles.
glasgow.building-use: Hillhead is a vibrant West End district of Glasgow characterised by a blend of academic, residential, religious and civic buildings. The University of Glasgow’s Gilmorehill campus, including landmarks such as the McMillan Reading Room, shapes much of the area’s identity. Historic tenements and terraces from the mid-nineteenth century contribute to its distinctive residential character. Overall, Hillhead combines academic institutions, historic housing, churches, schools and efficient transport, creating a dynamic and community-focused urban environment.
glasgow.character: The composition combines planimetric mapping with finely detailed elevations of notable buildings, including the main university complex and key civic and religious structures along the avenue. University Avenue forms the central spine, connecting Hillhead to the Gilmorehill campus, which illustrates the district’s identity as an academic hub. The drawing highlights both the monumental presence of university architecture and its integration within Glasgow’s historic urban fabric.
glasgow.room: Classic sandstone tenement is part of the terraced houses along Kersland Street. Although very little is known about the original plan, it is possible that some internal walls might have been reconfigured. The current flat features two bedrooms and a living area with a spacious bay window kitchen/dining, ideal as a shared student accommodation or a young family dwelling.

plock.population: The study records 19,863 residents across 2.42 km² of the neighbourhood.
plock.location: Wielka Płyta and Tysiąclecia, while separated on administrative level, have a common origin of a neighbourhood masterplanned and build for a specific purpose – housing workers of the newly built oil refinery and their families. What made those areas stand out was the premeditated inclusion of social infrastructure and room for further development. They were also chosen to be a part of the Lexicon due to one of the authors’ personal relationship to them.
plock.history: The neighbourhood was almost entirely planned and built between 1963 and 1970, during the transformation of the city into an industrial centre and the construction of the oil refinery. Before the construction of the neighbourhood, the area had been occupied by orchards and agricultural fields. Since its completion, it has remained almost untouched, except for the addition of a few public buildings.
plock.green-space: The park at the centre of the area, Aleja Antoniego Roguckiego, is its most notable feature, practically uniting both neighbourhoods on an urban level. Additionally, each cluster of blocks has its own green space with a playground in the middle, to provide a space for interaction and respite for their inhabitants.
plock.transport: Built in the 1960s, when car ownership was low, the main transport methods within the neighbourhood remained oriented around public transit, bike routes and foot traffic. The neighbourhood is well connected with the city through a network of bus routes and a biking path. Additionally, most public spaces are accessible for pedestrians and located within a 15-minute walking distance.
plock.building-use: The neighbourhood is almost entirely residential, consisting of high-rise, 10- and 5- storey blocks, arranged into clusters. The public buildings are either pushed to one side, if they’re of commercial use, or are placed in its heart, if they’re part of social infrastructure.
plock.character: The neighbourhood is mainly residential, with most of its public life and pedestrian circulation centred around the park that cuts through it. The public infrastructure, like schools and kindergartens, is integrated into the neighbourhood and easily accessible to the residents. The church was added in the 1980’s, when the socio-political climate allowed for more public displays of faith than it had before and religion was an important aspect of life and resistance.
plock.room: The inhabitants of the neighbourhood initially were workers of the oil refinery and the local industry. Currently, those people still occupy the flats, which makes the elderly the main demographic. The layout of the tower blocks emphasises commonality. The flats mostly consist of two or three rooms, arranged in threes or fours around a common corridor, connecting to the main stairwell.

lucca.population: The study records 10,000 residents across 4.20 km² of the neighbourhood.
lucca.location: The city of Lucca is designed around a central walled neighborhood; this unique urban form illustrates a clear orientation towards religious buildings. The nodes of the city are church piazzas where the social activities are concentrated. The area within the walls is completely walkable, enriching urban life and activity on the streets. Even though the neighborhood is car free it remains well connected due to the train station on the walled periphery and the road that surrounds it. The wall forms a physical barrier from the rest of the city, in contrast, this does not isolate the neighborhood but creates a center point for the city.
lucca.history: Lucca’s city expansion started with the Roman grid (black) initial military and trading settlement. Next expansion occurred during the Middle Ages (gray) with a new outer wall and continued population growth. The most important expansion took place during the Renaissance (light gray) where the fortified wall that we see today was constructed, encasing the central neighbourhood of Lucca. Since then, the expansion has consisted of your typical low rise spread out urban sprawl.
lucca.green-space: The majority of green space in Lucca can be found on the east side of the neighbourhood, where the villas and gardens are located. The top of the wall hosts a tree-lined promenade and play parks. A large, manicured landscape surrounds the fortifications, creating a green barrier between the inner and outer wall.
lucca.transport: Due to Lucca’s strict car regulation, transport is heavily based around walking. Bus travel is Lucca’s primary form of public transport inside the wall. It includes connections to different churches, piazzas and the main bus station. Outside of the wall the bus routes continue to connect the whole Province of Lucca. The train station, located just outside the wall, allows the neighbourhood to be linked to the rest of the cities of northern Italy.
lucca.building-use: Due to the versatile nature of the neighbourhood it encourages rich character and diversity on the street. Vibrant commercial activity is driven into the interconnected piazzas. In comparison to the other analysed samples one can clearly identify the organic development of urban zoning.
lucca.character: Essential characteristics of Lucca are the piazzas and churches. This combination creates a valued meeting point for all residents. These spaces celebrate various occasions, whether it is a festival, a market, or a Sunday Mass.
lucca.room: Many of the buildings found in the walls of Lucca are blocks of flats typically between three or four storeys. The most common arrangement consists of ground floor hosting a shop and a top floor containing an attic studio flat. The flat plan shown above is an example of the conventional setup with three bedrooms, primarily designed for families.

freiburg.population: The study records 5,634 residents across 0.38 km² of the neighbourhood.
freiburg.location: What makes Vauban stand out is its sustainable and community-led character. Through a planned mix of co-housing, subsidized apartments, and private homes, the district accommodates diverse socio-economic groups and helps prevent gentrification. The high standard of life, strong sense of community, and safe environment meet inhabitants’ needs and make the district especially attractive to young families.
freiburg.history: Vauban is a neighbourhood in Freiburg, Germany, developed between 1990 and 2000 as a ‘sustainable model district’. The only existing structures around in the area around that time were post war barracks which in the new scheme were adapted as apartment blocks. Unlike traditional urban areas that evolve gradually over time, Vauban was comprehensively planned before its construction.
freiburg.green-space: The green spaces in the neighbourhood are mostly public and include several playgrounds for children. One of the largest natural areas nearby is the Black Forest that is located outside the eastern edge of the neighbourhood.
freiburg.transport: Vauban prioritises public transport as a main mode of commuting. The tram line that goes through the centre of the neighbourhood provides a link to the Freiburg city centre, complemented by several bus lines and the car-sharing system. This way the residents are able to limit their car usage or exclude it completely. Cycling is also widely embraced, emphasising the sustainable and active mobility of the area.
freiburg.building-use: The majority of the buildings in the neighbourhood are residential. Some of them have varying character with shops or cafes located on the ground floor. The district’s core principle is sustainability, therefore all houses were built according to low-energy standards and equipped with photovoltaic panels. Vauban is also served by a highly efficient co-generation plant that supplies renewable energy to the neighbourhood. The area also hosts the Student Village which along with family housing adds diversity to the population.
freiburg.character: One of the qualities of Vauban that makes it stand out is its car-free streets. Without the risk of passing vehicles the streets become reclaimed by the residents. Being able to play safely throughout the neighbourhood, children thrive in this environment.
freiburg.room: Apartments of this sustainable urban neighbourhood are subject to rigorous Passivhaus standards, contributing to the reduction of heat loss. This has a positive impact on both the environment and operational expenses. Due to the engagement of residents into the planning process of the neighbourhood, housing types present in the area are quite varied. Most of them are family oriented, with multiple bedrooms and a generous living zone, and have access to a form of outdoor space whether it’s a balcony or a shared garden.
